prompt: `kubectl top pods` answers `error: Metrics API not available` on a fresh cluster. What is missing?

choices.text: The kubelets do not measure anything yet
choices.why: Every kubelet measures its containers all the time.

choices.text: metrics-server
choices.why: Right. Nothing collects the numbers into the API until it is installed.

choices.text: A Prometheus server
choices.why: `kubectl top` reads `metrics.k8s.io`, which metrics-server serves.

choices.text: Requests on every pod
choices.why: Usage is measured whether or not a request exists.

prompt: How does a request for `/apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/nodes` reach metrics-server?

choices.text: Through an Ingress in `kube-system`
choices.why: No Ingress was installed in that lab.

choices.text: kubectl calls metrics-server's pod address directly
choices.why: kubectl only talks to the API server.

choices.text: An APIService routes it via the API server
choices.why: Right. The API server forwards the group; `v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io` points at the Service `kube-system/metrics-server`.

choices.text: etcd stores the metrics and the API server reads them
choices.why: Metrics never touch etcd; metrics-server keeps them in memory.

prompt: A guide says to add `--kubelet-insecure-tls` to metrics-server on kind. What did this lab do instead, and why?

choices.text: Nothing; kind's kubelets already had trusted certificates
choices.why: By default they sign their own, which is why the flag exists.

choices.text: Gave each kubelet a certificate signed by the CA
choices.why: Right. Verification stays on; the flag would accept any certificate, including an impostor's.

choices.text: It used plain HTTP to the kubelets
choices.why: The arguments show `--secure-port` and HTTPS throughout.

choices.text: It turned off authentication on the API server
choices.why: Nothing in the lab touches the API server's authentication.

prompt: Each idle copy of the shop requested 500m and used about 1m. What did the other 499m cost?

choices.text: Nothing, because unused CPU is free
choices.why: Reserved CPU cannot be promised to another pod.

choices.text: The pod was throttled to 1m
choices.why: It had no CPU limit; it used 1m because it was idle.

choices.text: Capacity no other pod could get
choices.why: Right. The scheduler counts requests, so the reserve is spent whether used or not.

choices.text: Extra memory for the kubelet
choices.why: A CPU request reserves CPU only.

prompt: Under load the shop used up to 404m of CPU and at most 7 MiB of memory, against requests of 500m and 256 MiB. Which request was further off?

choices.text: Memory
choices.why: Right. About thirty times too much, against roughly right for CPU.

choices.text: CPU
choices.why: 500m against 404m is a modest margin.

choices.text: Both equally
choices.why: One was near and one was thirty times over.

choices.text: Neither; idle numbers are what count
choices.why: A request has to cover the pod working.

prompt: A team sets requests from one `kubectl top` reading taken on a quiet afternoon. What is the risk?
hint: How much history does metrics-server keep?

choices.text: None; `kubectl top` averages the last day
choices.why: It shows one recent sample; there is no daily average.

choices.text: The numbers are in the wrong units
choices.why: Millicores and bytes are the units requests use.

choices.text: The busy hours never get measured
choices.why: Right. Requests need the peaks over days, which a monitoring system stores.

choices.text: metrics-server rejects readings older than an hour
choices.why: It keeps only the newest set, but rejects nothing.
